newsitem.title: GERMANY: Government demand holds German call money in check.
newsitem.headline: Government demand holds German call money in check.

text.p: The German overnight call money rate was little changed at around 3.10 percent in quiet trade on Tuesday, dealers said.
"It's pretty much the same," said one trader. "There is some demand here and there."

Demand from the government stabilised call rates despite substantial liquidity, traders said. With such demand likely to continue in coming weeks, rates are unlikely to dip much below the 3.10 percent level. The trader said the government would continue to seek financing until the Bundesbank's profits are transferred on April 17.
"There are always periods when the government has expenditure needs," said a trader. "But in the current liquid environment, that demand is unlikey to upset the market."
He said ample reserve levels meant banks were reasonably willing to offer funds, meaning rates were not being pushed up as much as they would be in a less liquid situation.
Several banks predicted that the government's requirements in the coming weeks would be around 10 to 15 billion marks.
In its repo allocation, the Bundesbank is expected to about evenly match the 84.0 billion marks of securities repurchase agreements which expire on Wednesday.
"With call rates at 3.10 percent, the Bundesbank will be cautious about tightening up the market," said the trader.
"They will probably try to keep the market fairly neutral with this operation."
On Monday, banks held 42.1 billion marks in reserve at the Bundesbank, up from 41.1 billion held on Friday. Holdings for the month remained unchanged at 42.0 billion marks.
No appreciable amount was borrowed on the 4.50 percent Lombard financing window. The Frankfurt interbank overnight rate stood at 3.12567 percent versus 3.12633 on Monday.
